pass_b_english: Cyril: …brother should not draw near to you, nor should you set him over it, you will gather them inside into your house, and it will be with you until your brother should seek them, and you will give them back to him; thus you will do his donkey, and thus you will do his garment, and thus you will do according to every loss of your brother, whatever should be lost from him, and you should find, you will not be able to overlook them; you will not overlook the donkey of your brother, or his calf fallen in the way; do not overlook, raising you will raise them with him.’ You understand then how most urbanely he trains us toward the already somehow and perfectly good, commanding to make as it were a practice of not remembering evil—the sparing unto the beasts of the one who has grieved, whom he also crowns above and below with the name of brotherhood, checking, I think somewhere, the intense unto angers, and the superfluous unto smallness of soul, and bringing in the law of nature as somehow an umpire of love. For if you should find, he says, a wandering beast, or a lost garment, you will save them around for your brother; and if something of those accustomed to bear burdens should slip down to earth to be crushed under the load itself, you will work with and raise with. And this is nothing other than benefiting the owner, and a practice toward mercy, and a training toward love of one’s own, and seeking to push grief far away, and to decline differences, for the sake at least of not seeming to strike against love and the law unto brother-love. And it is likely that the oracular saying also somehow hints something other; for if such care has come about for the lawgiver, that even if something of the irrational should be what has suffered, he stretches out the help for us, how would the sparing unto humans, and the mutual love owed to those of like race, not please him more greatly? So even if an enemy should somehow wander, let him learn the straight way, and through us let him nod toward what benefits. Thus also Christ, though he was being struck with stones by those from Israel, was nevertheless calling out: ‘While you have the light, walk in the light, that darkness may not overtake you.’ And if someone of those who have struck against us should be squeezed in toil and trials, and somehow as thrown to earth should be pressed by inescapable necessities, he says, let him be helped by us, and let the differing one be better than grief. Or is this not the thing, ‘Do good to your enemies, and pray for those who insult you’?
Palladius: You have spoken most excellently.

Cyril: So then it is holy-fitting to suffer-with those who labor, and not rather to make the things upon which it was better to pity a pretext of grasping against them, still leaping upon and being angry at those who have been wronged.
